title: Blockchain Incentives
description: Proof of work, proof of stake, Sybil resistance, the cost of consensus

concepts.title: The Consensus Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you maintain a shared ledger without a central authority?

The challenge: anyone might lie. Without a trusted central record-keeper, you need a distributed mechanism that produces consensus despite some participants being dishonest.

This is the Byzantine Generals Problem from computer science. Classical solutions exist but require knowing all participants in advance.

Bitcoin's 2008 contribution: a consensus mechanism that works without identifying participants — anyone can join, anyone can leave, the system stays consistent. The economic incentive design is what makes it work.

The mechanism is elegant: the chain with the most accumulated work is the canonical history. To change the past, you'd need to redo more work than the rest of the network combined.

concepts.title: Proof of Work
concepts.contentHtml:
Bitcoin's Proof of Work (PoW): miners compete to solve cryptographic puzzles. Solving a puzzle gives the right to add the next block of transactions. The miner gets a reward (newly minted coins plus transaction fees).

The puzzles are deliberately hard — they require massive computation, electricity, and specialized hardware (ASICs).

Why this works:

– Sybil resistance: creating many identities doesn't help. What matters is computational power, which costs real money.

– Economic security: attacking the network requires controlling >50% of compute power, which is enormously expensive.

– Honesty incentive: miners are rewarded in the network's currency. Attacks that destroy trust in the network destroy the value of their rewards.

The cost: Bitcoin uses ~150 TWh/year — comparable to medium-sized countries. The economic security comes from real resource consumption.

concepts.title: Proof of Stake
concepts.contentHtml:
Proof of Stake (PoS) replaces computational competition with economic stake.

Validators lock up tokens as collateral ('stake'). The protocol selects validators to add blocks based partly on stake size. Honest behavior earns rewards; dishonest behavior loses staked tokens.

Ethereum transitioned from PoW to PoS in 2022 (the 'Merge'). Energy consumption fell ~99.95%.

Economic security in PoS comes from forfeitable stake rather than burnt resources. Attacking the network requires controlling >33% (some implementations) or >50% (others) of staked tokens. The attacker would lose those tokens through 'slashing' — protocol-imposed penalties for misbehavior.

Tradeoffs:

– PoW ties security to external resources (electricity, hardware). Hard to attack without obvious external footprint.

– PoS ties security to internal token economics. More energy-efficient but more complex governance.

The cryptocurrency community remains debated about which is preferable. The trend has been toward PoS as energy concerns have grown.

concepts.title: Mining Economics
concepts.contentHtml:
Bitcoin mining is a competitive industry with interesting economic dynamics.

The supply equation: each miner's expected revenue equals total network rewards times their share of total hash rate. If revenue exceeds operating cost (electricity, hardware depreciation), miners enter; if not, they exit.

The result: in equilibrium, mining profits are competed down to roughly cover operating costs. Bitcoin's hash rate adjusts to make mining unprofitable for the marginal miner — exactly as it should under competition.

This is also why mining gravitates to cheap electricity — Iceland (geothermal), Texas (oil/gas waste), China (until 2021 ban; hydroelectric in summer, coal in winter).

Mining centralization concerns: ASICs are expensive, available only from a few manufacturers. Mining pools concentrate hash rate. Whether Bitcoin's actual decentralization matches its theoretical promise is debated.

concepts.title: Cost of Decentralization
concepts.contentHtml:
Decentralized consensus has costs traditional payment systems don't have.

– Energy or capital: PoW burns electricity; PoS locks up capital. Either way, real resources are consumed for security.

– Speed: Bitcoin can process ~7 transactions per second. Visa handles ~65,000. The decentralization tradeoff is real.

– Storage: nodes must store the entire transaction history. Bitcoin's ledger is now well over 600GB and growing. Running a full node is increasingly expensive.

– Coordination: protocol changes require consensus among many parties. Bitcoin's history of contentious forks (Bitcoin Cash, Bitcoin SV) shows this isn't just theoretical.

The argument for decentralization: it provides censorship resistance, reduces single-points-of-failure, and creates financial infrastructure beyond government control.

The argument against: the costs may exceed benefits for most use cases. Centralized systems are faster, cheaper, and more user-friendly.

The most interesting cryptocurrency applications are where the decentralization premium is worth paying — adversarial environments, censorship resistance, financial inclusion in jurisdictions with weak institutions.

title: Token Design
description: Utility, governance, security tokens — bonding curves, vesting, sinks and faucets

concepts.title: What Tokens Represent
concepts.contentHtml:
A cryptocurrency token is a unit of account on a blockchain. Different tokens represent very different things.

Native cryptocurrencies: Bitcoin, Ether — base units of their networks.

Stablecoins: USDC, USDT, DAI — tokens designed to maintain a peg to fiat or other assets.

Utility tokens: grant access to a service or platform. Filecoin (storage), Helium (wireless network), Render (compute).

Governance tokens: grant voting rights in protocol decisions. Uniswap (UNI), Maker (MKR), Compound (COMP).

Security tokens: represent ownership of underlying assets — equity, debt, real estate. Often regulated as securities.

NFTs: non-fungible tokens representing unique items — digital art, collectibles, identity, certificates.

Each type has different economics and regulatory implications.

concepts.title: Token Supply Mechanisms
concepts.contentHtml:
How are tokens created and distributed? Several models.

Fixed supply: Bitcoin's 21 million cap. Disinflationary by design — supply growth slows over time.

Predictable issuance: Ethereum has variable issuance based on validator activity but with built-in deflationary pressure (EIP-1559 burn mechanism).

Algorithmic supply: stablecoins like Terra (before collapse) tried algorithmic supply expansion/contraction to maintain pegs.

Inflationary: some tokens issue continuously to fund development or pay validators (Cosmos, Solana).

Bonding curves: the price of a token is mathematically tied to its supply. As demand rises, supply expands at a rising price.

Each model creates different incentives. Fixed-supply tokens encourage hoarding; inflationary tokens encourage spending. Bonding curves provide automated market-making.

concepts.title: Sinks and Faucets
concepts.contentHtml:
Token economies, like videogames, need sinks (where tokens are consumed) and faucets (where tokens are issued).

Faucets: mining rewards, staking rewards, liquidity mining payouts, airdrops.

Sinks: transaction fees, protocol fees, token burns, governance staking, locked collateral.

Without sufficient sinks, tokens become inflationary as faucets keep adding supply. Without sufficient faucets, the economy can't grow or attract participation.

Examples:

– Ethereum's EIP-1559 burns base transaction fees, creating a sink that can exceed issuance during high activity.

– MakerDAO (now Sky) used surplus stability-fee revenue, paid in DAI, to buy back and burn MKR, creating deflationary pressure proportional to system usage.

– BNB's quarterly burns reduce supply over time.

Token economics is a young field. Many projects design naively, end up with hyperinflation or stagnation. Better designs have learned from videogame and economic theory.

concepts.title: Vesting and Distribution
concepts.contentHtml:
How tokens are initially distributed shapes long-run dynamics.

Fair launch: like Bitcoin's early mining or Dogecoin — anyone can mine; founders don't pre-allocate.

ICO/IPO-style: early sales to investors. Typical of 2017-era ICOs. Often subject to SEC scrutiny in the US as unregistered securities offerings.

Airdrops: free distribution to existing users (Uniswap's UNI airdrop to past users, worth ~$1,200 at launch and far more at peak). Bootstrap network effects without explicit sales.

Liquidity mining: tokens distributed to users who provide liquidity to protocols. Drove much DeFi growth in 2020-21.

Vesting schedules:

Token allocations to founders, employees, and early investors typically vest over years to align incentives. Cliff vesting (no tokens for the first year, then linear release) is standard.

Without vesting: founders can dump tokens immediately after launch, crashing prices. With long vesting: founders are aligned with long-term success.

concepts.title: Token Velocity
concepts.contentHtml:
The velocity of money — how fast tokens circulate — affects token value.

From the equation of exchange: MV = PT, where M is token supply, V is velocity, P is price level (in fiat), T is transaction volume (in fiat).

Solving for token value: M·P_token = T/V, where P_token is token price in fiat.

If transaction volume T grows but velocity V grows too (because people use tokens immediately for transactions), token price can stagnate even with rising adoption.

This is the velocity problem for utility tokens. If users buy tokens, transact, and immediately sell, velocity is high and token price is low.

Solutions involve creating reasons to hold tokens beyond just transacting:

– Staking yields incentivize holding rather than spending.

– Governance rights give holders ongoing influence.

– Discounts or fee rebates for token holders.

– Required collateral for protocol functions.

Successful token economies engineer multiple reasons to hold. Failed ones optimize for transactions alone and watch prices stagnate or fall despite usage growth.

title: DeFi Primitives
description: AMMs, lending protocols, liquidity mining, impermanent loss

concepts.title: What DeFi Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Decentralized Finance (DeFi) rebuilds traditional financial services — exchange, lending, insurance, derivatives — on blockchains, without traditional intermediaries.

Smart contracts (programmable code on blockchains) enforce the rules. There's no human banker, no central exchange, no insurance company in the middle. The contract executes deterministically; users interact directly with code.

The 2020-21 'DeFi summer' saw rapid growth. Total value locked in DeFi protocols peaked near $180 billion in late 2021 (DefiLlama). After the 2022-23 bear market, the sector remains substantial — $50-100 billion locked across protocols.

The core appeal: financial services without permission, available 24/7, transparent (anyone can verify code), and accessible to anyone with internet access.

concepts.title: Automated Market Makers
concepts.contentHtml:
How do you run an exchange without an order book?

Automated Market Makers (AMMs), pioneered by Uniswap (2018), use liquidity pools and a mathematical pricing formula.

Setup: liquidity providers (LPs) deposit pairs of tokens (e.g., ETH and USDC) into a pool. The protocol uses a formula — most commonly x · y = k — to determine swap prices.

If you want to swap ETH for USDC, the protocol sells you USDC at a price determined by the current pool ratio. Your trade changes the ratio, which changes the price.

This is elegant: no need to match buyers and sellers, no order books, no central matching engine. The pool is always available; trades execute against the formula.

Constraints: prices on AMMs can deviate from external markets. Arbitrageurs profit by aligning AMM prices with external prices, which keeps the system roughly correct.

Uniswap, Curve, Balancer, and other AMMs handle hundreds of billions in volume. The model has been so successful that even traditional finance is exploring AMM-style mechanisms for some illiquid markets.

concepts.title: Lending Protocols
concepts.contentHtml:
DeFi lending works through over-collateralized loans.

Setup: a borrower deposits collateral (say, $1500 worth of ETH) and borrows up to some fraction (say, $1000 in USDC). If the collateral value falls below a threshold, it's automatically liquidated to repay the loan.

Lenders earn interest on their deposited tokens. Interest rates float based on supply and demand within the pool.

Major protocols: Aave, Compound, MakerDAO. Each has variations in collateral types, interest rate models, and risk parameters.

Why over-collateralization? Because the protocol can't enforce traditional credit (no credit scores, no legal recourse against pseudonymous addresses). Over-collateralization protects the lender if the borrower defaults — the collateral covers the loan.

This means DeFi lending today is essentially leveraged trading. People borrow against crypto collateral to buy more crypto. Real-world unsecured lending, with all its credit-risk pricing, hasn't translated to DeFi.

concepts.title: Liquidity Mining
concepts.contentHtml:
Liquidity mining: protocols reward users for providing liquidity by issuing native tokens.

Compound launched the model in 2020 with COMP token rewards. Users earned both interest on deposits and additional COMP tokens. Massive capital flowed in seeking the combined yield.

The mechanism: bootstrap a network through token incentives. Distribute ownership to early users. Create deep liquidity that attracts more users.

Critique: 'mercenary capital.' Yields chase rewards, then exit when rewards stop. Many liquidity-mining schemes attracted capital that vanished when token rewards ended.

Better designs offer time-locks, escalating rewards for committed liquidity, or revenue-sharing rather than pure inflation rewards.

The concept echoes Hayek's 'denationalization of money' arguments — multiple competing currencies (now tokens) bidding for adoption. The reality has been messier, with substantial misallocation but also rapid innovation in financial primitives.

concepts.title: Impermanent Loss
concepts.contentHtml:
A peculiar feature of providing liquidity to AMMs: impermanent loss.

Setup: you provide $1000 of ETH and $1000 of USDC to a Uniswap pool. ETH rises 4×. The pool rebalances; you end up with less ETH and more USDC.

Comparison: if you'd just held the original ETH and USDC, you'd have $4000 ETH + $1000 USDC = $5000.

Actual outcome from the pool: you have ~$4000 worth of tokens (the pool rebalanced you out of ETH as it rose). Less than just holding.

The gap is impermanent loss — 'impermanent' because if prices return to the original ratio, the loss disappears. 'Permanent' if prices stay diverged.

Liquidity providers earn fees from trades to compensate for IL. Whether fees outweigh IL depends on volatility and trading volume.

The concept is widely misunderstood — many liquidity providers don't realize they're effectively short volatility. More sophisticated AMM designs (Uniswap V3 concentrated liquidity, Curve's stable pools) try to mitigate IL for specific use cases.

title: MEV & Mechanism Risks
description: Maximal extractable value, front-running, sandwich attacks, fair ordering

concepts.title: What MEV Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Maximal Extractable Value (MEV) — formerly Miner Extractable Value — is the value that block producers can extract from users by exploiting their privileged position in transaction ordering.

The mechanism: when you submit a transaction to a blockchain, it sits in a public mempool waiting to be included in a block. The block producer (miner in PoW, validator in PoS) decides which transactions to include and in what order.

This power isn't trivial. Order can determine profits. Smart actors competing for limited transaction slots create elaborate strategies to extract value.

Estimated MEV extracted on Ethereum since 2020: $700+ million. The actual figure may be substantially higher when factoring in less-visible forms.

concepts.title: Front-Running
concepts.contentHtml:
The simplest MEV strategy: front-running.

Setup: you see a large pending transaction in the mempool. You submit a similar transaction with a higher gas fee (higher priority) so yours executes first. You profit from the price impact your front-run trade caused.

This is illegal in traditional finance. In crypto, it's not — anyone can see the mempool, anyone can pay for higher priority. The asymmetry between sophisticated bots and ordinary users is structural.

Real-world impact: large DeFi trades pay an implicit 'tax' to MEV bots. A retail trader trying to swap a meaningful amount on Uniswap gets a worse price because bots front-run them.

Defensive techniques: private mempools (Flashbots Protect, MEV Blocker), batch auctions, time delays. None fully eliminate MEV; they shift who captures it.

concepts.title: Sandwich Attacks
concepts.contentHtml:
A more sophisticated MEV strategy: the sandwich attack.

Setup: you see a victim's pending swap that will move the AMM price. Your bot:

1. Front-runs: buys the asset before the victim, raising its price.

2. The victim's swap executes at the now-worse price.

3. Back-runs: sells the asset right after, profiting from the temporary price move you created.

The victim pays substantial slippage. The attacker captures the spread.

Sandwich attacks are pervasive on Ethereum mainnet. Cumulative damages to users are estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars.

User defenses: setting tight slippage tolerances (which can cause failed transactions), using private routing services, using stable pools that resist sandwiching by design.

concepts.title: Arbitrage and Liquidations
concepts.contentHtml:
Not all MEV is malicious. Some is legitimate market-making.

Arbitrage: when DEX prices diverge from CEX prices, bots profit by aligning them. Total MEV from arbitrage: hundreds of millions per year. Without it, DEX prices would diverge persistently from external markets.

Liquidations: when DeFi loans fall below collateral thresholds, bots execute liquidations and earn fees. Without timely liquidations, lending protocols would suffer bad debt.

These activities provide market services. The bots earn returns by performing them. The economic cost is partly inefficient — bots compete with each other, often paying most of their profits in gas — but the underlying functions are valuable.

The line between 'predatory' MEV (extracting value from users without service) and 'legitimate' MEV (providing market services) is blurry. Most complex MEV strategies do some of each.

concepts.title: MEV Mitigation
concepts.contentHtml:
The crypto community has developed several approaches to limit harmful MEV.

Flashbots: a private auction system where bundle proposers compete to include MEV transactions. This concentrates MEV extraction but reduces user-visible impact.

Proposer-builder separation (PBS): Ethereum's roadmap separates block proposing (validator) from block building (specialized builders). Reduces validator-level MEV concentration.

Batch auctions: protocols like CoW Swap aggregate user trades into batches with uniform clearing prices, eliminating order-dependent MEV.

Encrypted mempools: hide pending transactions until ordering is finalized. Hard to implement but theoretically eliminates much MEV.

Single-block proposers: reduce MEV opportunities by making block-building atomic with proposing.

The MEV problem is one of the most active research areas in crypto. It exposes a fundamental tension: blockchain transparency (anyone can see pending transactions) creates exactly the conditions for value extraction. Solving it requires either changing the transparency model or designing mechanisms that internalize MEV in welfare-improving ways.

title: Stablecoins & Monetary Theory
description: Fiat-backed, crypto-backed, algorithmic — the Terra collapse and what stability requires

concepts.title: Why Stablecoins Exist
concepts.contentHtml:
Cryptocurrencies are volatile. Bitcoin can move 10% in a day. This makes them poor mediums of exchange — buyers and sellers don't want a unit of account that swings widely.

Stablecoins are tokens designed to maintain a stable value, typically pegged to a fiat currency (most often the US dollar).

Use cases:

– DeFi base currency: stable lending, predictable trade pairs.

– Cross-border payments: faster and cheaper than traditional remittances.

– Inflation hedge in unstable economies: USDC use in Argentina, Turkey, parts of Africa.

– Trading liquidity: moving between volatile crypto and stable value within crypto markets.

Total stablecoin market cap: about $300 billion by 2026, up from ~$160 billion in early 2024.

concepts.title: Fiat-Backed Stablecoins
concepts.contentHtml:
The simplest model: fiat-backed stablecoins. The issuer holds dollar reserves equal to outstanding tokens. One token = one dollar redeemable.

Major examples:

USDT (Tether): first major stablecoin. Long-running concerns about reserve quality and transparency. Roughly $180B in circulation in 2026.

USDC (Circle): regulated, with monthly reserve attestations, backed by cash and short-term Treasuries. Roughly $75B in 2026.

BUSD (Binance): previously regulated by NYDFS. Wound down 2023.

The economic logic is straightforward: it's effectively a money-market fund issued as crypto tokens. The risk is whether the issuer actually holds claimed reserves.

Reserve transparency has improved over time. USDC publishes monthly attestations showing reserve composition. Tether resisted full transparency for years; recent attestations show predominantly Treasury bills.

Regulatory framework is evolving. The EU's MiCA regulation imposed strict reserve requirements. In the US, the GENIUS Act (signed July 2025) set a federal framework for payment stablecoins.

concepts.title: Crypto-Backed Stablecoins
concepts.contentHtml:
Some stablecoins use cryptocurrency collateral instead of fiat reserves.

DAI is the canonical example. Users deposit ETH (or other approved crypto) at over-collateralization (typically 150-300%) and mint DAI tokens against it.

Advantages: more decentralized than fiat-backed; doesn't require trust in a specific issuer.

Disadvantages: capital-inefficient (need much more collateral than tokens issued); vulnerable to collateral price crashes (March 2020 ETH crash nearly broke DAI).

Hybrid approaches: DAI now backs partially with USDC (a fiat-backed stablecoin), reintroducing some centralization but improving stability.

The economic logic resembles classic banking: assets (crypto collateral) back liabilities (DAI tokens). Solvency requires maintaining over-collateralization through volatile markets — challenging during crashes.

concepts.title: Algorithmic Stablecoins and the Terra Collapse
concepts.contentHtml:
The most ambitious — and most catastrophic — stablecoin design: algorithmic stablecoins.

Idea: maintain peg through programmatic supply adjustments rather than reserves. When the stablecoin trades above peg, mint more; when below, contract supply.

UST (TerraUSD) was the largest such project. By early 2022, UST had a market cap of ~$18B, supported by a sister token LUNA. The mechanism: users could always swap 1 UST for $1 worth of LUNA, and vice versa.

The collapse (May 2022): a large UST sell-off triggered LUNA inflation as the protocol minted LUNA to absorb UST. As LUNA price fell, the math broke. UST de-pegged. The death spiral consumed both tokens within a week. Both went to near-zero. ~$60 billion of value evaporated.

The lesson: algorithmic stability without reserves is structurally fragile. The mechanism only works while market participants believe it works. Once belief erodes, the spiral is self-reinforcing.

Many algorithmic stablecoins have failed since (USN/Near, USDD, others). The category is now widely viewed with skepticism. Future designs may add partial reserves to algorithmic mechanisms.

concepts.title: Stablecoins as Monetary Phenomenon
concepts.contentHtml:
Stablecoins now hold roughly $300B in dollar-denominated reserves, mostly in US Treasuries. They're effectively private dollar issuers.

Implications:

– Demand for Treasuries: stablecoins are a major non-trivial buyer of T-bills, supporting Treasury demand.

– Monetary policy transmission: stablecoin reserves earn interest rate; the spread funds operations and may pass through to users (some stablecoins now offer yield).

– Dollar dominance: ~99% of stablecoins are USD-pegged. Stablecoins extend dollar use globally, potentially counter to local monetary sovereignty.

– Financial stability: a 'run' on a major stablecoin could disrupt Treasury markets, given the concentration of reserves.

– Privacy and surveillance: dollar use via stablecoins is at least somewhat traceable through blockchain analytics, with implications for capital controls.

Regulatory developments: the US Federal Reserve, EU, and major regulators are all developing stablecoin frameworks. Most aim to maintain stability while limiting systemic risks. The eventual settled architecture isn't clear.

Whatever the final form, stablecoins represent a significant innovation in private monetary arrangements — the most successful new form of money since money market funds, with similar regulatory and stability questions.
